title: A weaned child (Psalm 131)
hook: I've calmed and quieted my soul like a weaned child with its mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, De profundis, out of the depths, and your line, more than watchmen for morning.

Watch a nursing baby on a parent's lap. All need: rooting, fussing, grabbing, turning toward the one thing it wants, crying until it gets it. Nothing wrong with that; that's what babies are for. Now watch an older child on the same lap. Weaned. Not hungry, not asking for anything. Just leaning back against a parent's chest, legs dangling, watching the room. Heavy and calm. There because it's a good place to be, and for no other reason. Same lap, same parent, a completely different way of being held. A psalm only three verses long is about that difference.
screen: `A NURSING BABY: ALL NEED.` → `A WEANED CHILD: JUST LEANING.` → `THE SAME LAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty-one is three verses long. Here's the first, in the King James Bible: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me." Haughty means lifted up. Lofty eyes are eyes always looking above their station. And exercise myself means busy myself, chase after. The writer has stopped straining after things too big to grasp. Not because they don't matter, but because they're not his to carry. Then verse two: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child." In the book of Samuel, Hannah keeps her boy at home until he's weaned, and only then brings him to the temple. So a weaned child isn't a newborn. It's a small person who no longer needs the breast, and yet still climbs into its mother's lap. That's the picture of the soul here. Not empty of desire. Quieted. With God, not to get something, just to be there. The writer says he did this himself: I have behaved and quieted myself. It took effort to get still. Then the last verse turns outward again, like Psalm one hundred thirty did: "Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever." It's another song of going up, and the heading gives it to David. Some Christian contemplatives use this little psalm as a picture of prayer that asks for nothing.
screen: `NOT HAUGHTY, NOT LOFTY` · `THINGS TOO HIGH FOR ME` · `WEANED: NOT HUNGRY, STILL HELD` · `I HAVE QUIETED MYSELF` · then, large: `MY SOUL IS EVEN AS A WEANED CHILD.`

segments.voice: Set down every request for now: no list, no fixing, no improving yourself, and if something you want comes to mind, let it go by. Lean back into the chair the way a child leans against a parent, and let your breathing be heavy and slow. If you pray, simply rest in God's presence, wordless, like the child in the lap; if you don't, just rest, asking nothing of the minute.
Hannah. The mother in the book of Samuel who kept her son home until he was weaned, the picture behind this psalm's quiet, grown-up trust.
Your line: quieted, like a child. Still wanting, but leaning back at last. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 436 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON.`

howItsDone: Christians in contemplative traditions often pray Psalm 131 before silent prayer, and it is sung at evening prayer in many churches and monasteries.

chat.says: Psalm 131 compares the soul to a weaned child. Why weaned, and not a newborn?
options: A weaned child isn't hungry, but still climbs into the lap: with God just to be there.
A newborn can't talk yet, and the psalm wants the soul to ask God for more things.
The soul should outgrow needing God, the way a child outgrows needing its mother.
chat.meaning: A weaned child no longer nurses, yet still leans on its mother. The soul here isn't empty of desire, just quieted, with God simply to be there.

lofty.meaning: high; here, eyes looking above their station
